You would think having mastery over magic might mean he had a fucking brain, but apparently that was too much to ask. The only reason he didn't have a knife in his back is because magi were useful for this sort of basterdly work. Instead of bumbling in the woods for weeks with multiple scouting parties you could send one with a magi, since they appeared to have the ability to locate a caravan easily given it came within a few miles.

His teeth attempted to turn each other into dust just thinking about how it was done. Baletik had only been near heavy magic use a handful of times but that was enough to know he hated it. Instead of continuing that train of thought he shielded his eyes from the light and detached from the group trying very hard to blend in with the surrounded trees and shrubs as he waited for the shitstorm that was sure to follow such a blatant betrayal of their presence...

Edit: Things

I can definitely get behind the core idea of your vignette: a scouting party bumbling around in dark and wicked woods with a fool of a magician waving around some bright red light for the entirely pleasant denizens of the forest to see; the suspense as the reader cowers from the creeping and crawling horrors that are bound to devour their party alive...

Something that would make the post stronger is adding more details. What is the narrator fearing? Building off of your worldbuilding, are there any renowned creatures of which there are already tales? What happened to past travelers?

That being said, I do think that the abrupt entrance brings a nice sense of brevity and alarm into the work. Good job!
I appreciate the feedback and can only really say: I felt like because it was so short that if I tried to cram a lot of extra detail in it might detract from the feel of the story.

First off, thanks for taking my advice well! If I'm being overbearing at all please correct me -- it isn't my intention to do anything but proffer a good critique.

The fundamental issue, however, is the ratio of exposition to actual narrative itself. Every large paragraph is almost entirely the narrator telling the reader how they got into that perilous situation; only light details regarding what he's actually fearing are present, which makes the job of imagining these nasties difficult for the reader, deprived of any reference points for their fears.

I would recommend adding a hearty amount of detail -- in this case, the fear of what's going to happen would be well worth the narrative plumbing.
Not bad. I'd like to hear more about how he meets and kills his ancestors.

Summer nights in my village are best spent outside the woods. The way the Adirondacks fill with haze around witching hour should be enough to keep people away. Deceiving moonlight makes the vastness appear manageable, but most people find themselves lost soon after they enter. Trees and hills seem to move around you. We warned the children to stay away first. Though the hunters and hikers have now given up their games.

There are things out there. Well, people, but we hardly consider them human. Of course, they must exist during the daylight. It would be silly to think they don't. However, it's sillier to try finding them. We've tried that. Door to door searched of every home in town turned up nothing suspicious. If it's one of our neighbors they have they're...gear hidden quite well.

Three weekends ago the Williams' boy went camping with a group of his friends. The Williams have thirty acres behind their home that their kids explored on the weekends. Five fifteen year-old boys entered the woods. Technically one returned; comatose with skin that tore at the slightest touch. He passed away in a hospital two days later. Some would argue his fate was kinder than his friends'.

The other four boys, including the Williams' son, were found murdered. Their bodies were stacked inside the tent. Each one had a single incision from the hollow of their throat to the groin. Empty sockets took the place of several organs, including the hearts and livers. Autopsies revealed that the boys were still alive through most of the slaughter.

Search parties scoured the woods for a week. Nobody turned up. Hunters and hikers returned to the trees. Those like the Williams, who owned a lot of woodland property, put up trail cams. SD cards quickly filled with suspicious images. Red lights glowing off in the distance.

Most people think it's a hoax, inspired by the horrific murders that took place a month ago. They might be right. I think I'll just stay inside at night.
